summary:
MISSION CONTROL is a cooperative multiplayer game for up to 5 players on one local network, built in Godot 4.7 by Team Pawstronauts. Four players on four laptops take the roles of FLIGHT, SYSTEMS, PAYLOAD, and GROUND, and a fifth screen runs Mission Control for the whole room. Each crew member sees only part of the numbers, so they have to talk to fit one spacecraft onto one rocket and one budget. They then launch it and survive in-flight crises using the spare margins they built into the design. Empty seats are flown by AI crew bots, so 1 to 5 people can play.


It addresses the challenge by turning real mission-design practice into something anyone can play. Players face the same trade-offs between mass, power, cost, risk, and science value that NASA teams negotiate, including Design Review go/no-go calls and Radio Silence communication blackouts. It matters because it shows that spacecraft are built by teams, not by one person, and that good margins and clear communication make missions succeed. It runs offline and includes plain-language hints, so classrooms and beginners can use it easily.
details:
MISSION CONTROL is a cooperative multiplayer game for up to 5 players on one local network. It teaches how real space missions are designed.

What it does: Four players sit at four laptops as FLIGHT, SYSTEMS, PAYLOAD, and GROUND, and a fifth screen runs Mission Control for the whole room. Each crew member sees only part of the numbers, so the team must talk to fit one spacecraft onto one rocket and one budget. They pick parts, hold a Design Review where everyone votes GO or NO-GO, then launch and handle in-flight crises by playing cards and passing tokens to teammates. A debrief gives a grade, medals, and a mission patch. Empty seats are flown by AI crew bots, so 1 to 5 people can play.

Benefits and impact: Players learn that every spacecraft is a negotiation between mass, power, cost, risk, and science value, and that spare margins and clear communication save missions. It needs only laptops and a router, so it works in classrooms without internet. Plain-language hints and a coach that suggests the next fix keep it friendly for beginners and younger players.

Tools: We built it in Godot 4.7 using GDScript, with LAN multiplayer over Godot’s networking. Game data lives in JSON, and automated tests check the design math. Sound effects and music are generated from code with Python, so there is no third-party audio. The team made the artwork, including four cat astronaut crew portraits.

Creativity: Each player has a secret goal, a ping wheel replaces chat during Radio Silence crises, and the chat beep imitates Apollo-era Quindar tones.

Factors considered: Teamwork, accessibility, offline play, and balanced difficulty. The numbers are game-scale and not official NASA data.

AI assistance: The team used Claude to help draft code, merge modules, and balance numbers.
